name: benethos-lexware-office-mcp
description: Unofficial MCP server for the Lexware Office accounting API — runs over stdio or HTTP.
long_description: Not affiliated with Lexware. **Nothing is enabled after installing** but `server_status`, which says what is running. Pick the prompt **Set up Lexware Office** under the plus in the message box: it opens the configuration interface in your browser, where you enter the API key and decide which tools exist. Both apply at once. A key changed later applies after quitting Claude Desktop from the tray and starting it again.

prompts.name: open_items
prompts.description: What is still unpaid, owed to the company and owed by it, overdue first.
prompts.text:
List what is still unpaid in the books. Contact filter: "${arguments.contact}". When the filter is empty, cover every contact.

Use only the tools in your list. The account owner decides which exist, so when one named here is missing, say which one and that it can be enabled in the configuration, and leave out the step that needs it rather than working around it.

1. When the contact filter is not empty, find the contact with `search_contacts` by name and take the `id` of the match. When several match, list them and ask which one is meant before going on. When none matches, say so and stop.
2. Call `search_vouchers` with voucher_status open and size 250, with the contact's id as contact_id when there is one. Open covers what is overdue as well. Leave out every row whose `voucherType` is quotation, orderconfirmation or deliverynote: an open quotation owes nothing.
3. Sort the rest by direction. invoice, salesinvoice and downpaymentinvoice are owed to the company, and creditnote and salescreditnote reduce that. purchaseinvoice is owed by the company, and purchasecreditnote reduces that.

Then report two tables, owed to the company and owed by it. Each has a row per contact with the number of documents, the sum of `openAmount` per currency, the earliest `dueDate` and how many days that lies before today. Contacts with something overdue come first, the longest overdue on top. A row without `openAmount` counts with its `totalAmount`, marked as such. Below each table, list the overdue documents one by one with number, date, due date and open amount, each with a link from `get_deeplink`, which costs no API call: the target is the document type for invoice (invoice), creditnote (credit-note) and downpaymentinvoice (down-payment-invoice), and voucher for the bookkeeping types.

Ids come from a search result, never from memory. Amounts are exactly what Lexware reports, each with its currency, never rounded and never converted, and a sum is formed per currency. A list answers in pages: read the `page` block and ask for the next page only while `last` is false. Every call spends from one budget of two requests per second. This is a reading task: change nothing in the books, even where a fix looks obvious, and name every gap in the data rather than filling it with a guess. Give no tax advice.

prompts.name: missing_receipts
prompts.description: Which receipt or invoice a period lacks, by the rhythm of the year before.
prompts.text:
Check the books for receipts and invoices missing in the period "${arguments.period}". It is a month such as 2026-10, a quarter such as 2026-Q3, or a year. When it is empty, take the last complete month before today.

Use only the tools in your list. The account owner decides which exist, so when one named here is missing, say which one and that it can be enabled in the configuration, and leave out the step that needs it rather than working around it.

1. Fix the first and the last day of the period. The history is the twelve months before its first day.
2. Call `search_vouchers` with date_from the first day of the history, date_to the last day of the period, sort voucherDate,ASC and size 250, and page through to the end. Leave out every row whose `voucherType` is quotation, orderconfirmation or deliverynote, and every row whose `voucherStatus` is voided.
3. Call `get_recurring_templates`. A contact with a template whose `executionStatus` says it still runs is invoiced on its schedule, which `recurringTemplateSettings` carries.

Work by these fixed rules, so that the same books always give the same answer.

- Groups. One group per `contactName` and direction. Incoming are purchaseinvoice and purchasecreditnote, outgoing every other type. A row without a contact name belongs to no group. When one group holds two amounts that recur side by side, two contracts with the same supplier for instance, split it by `totalAmount`, within ten percent.
- Rhythm, read from the history alone by `voucherDate`. Monthly: a voucher in at least four of the last six months of the history. Quarterly, when not monthly: a voucher in at least three of its last four quarters. Yearly, when neither: one voucher in the history, dated twelve months before a month of the period. One year is a single observation, so mark that rhythm as weak. Any other group has no rhythm and is not reported as missing.
- Expected. Monthly in every month of the period. Quarterly in each month of the period that lies a multiple of three months after the group's last voucher. Yearly in the month twelve months after it. A voucher dated in that month, or up to ten days either side of it, meets it.
- Not due yet. An expected month that has not ended by today is not missing, list it as not due yet.
- Ended. When the expected voucher is missing in the two months or quarters before the period as well, the rhythm has likely ended, a contract cancelled. List the group as possibly ended rather than missing.
- Templates. An outgoing group with a running template is expected as its schedule says. A missing invoice there means the template did not run, say so.
- Unfinished. Every row dated in the period with `voucherStatus` draft or unchecked is open still, whatever its rhythm.

Then report, in this order: what is missing, as a table with contact, direction, rhythm, the usual amount, the month expected, and the number and date of the last voucher with a link from `get_deeplink`, which costs no API call: the target is the document type for invoice (invoice), creditnote (credit-note) and downpaymentinvoice (down-payment-invoice), and voucher for the bookkeeping types. Then the unfinished vouchers of the period, with their links. Then the groups possibly ended, and those not due yet. Last, one line per group whose rhythm was met, so the person sees what was checked. A rhythm is a hint and not a fact: a missing voucher may never have been issued, so ask about it rather than asserting it is lost.

Ids come from a search result, never from memory. Amounts are exactly what Lexware reports, each with its currency, never rounded and never converted, and a sum is formed per currency. A list answers in pages: read the `page` block and ask for the next page only while `last` is false. Every call spends from one budget of two requests per second. This is a reading task: change nothing in the books, even where a fix looks obvious, and name every gap in the data rather than filling it with a guess. Give no tax advice.

prompts.name: contact_overview
prompts.description: One customer or vendor: the record, the latest documents, what is open.
prompts.text:
Give an overview of the contact "${arguments.contact}".

Use only the tools in your list. The account owner decides which exist, so when one named here is missing, say which one and that it can be enabled in the configuration, and leave out the step that needs it rather than working around it.

1. Find the contact with `search_contacts`: by number when the contact is given as digits only, by name otherwise. When several match, list them and ask which one is meant before going on. When none matches, say so and stop.
2. Call `get_contact` with its `id`.
3. Call `search_vouchers` with the id as contact_id and size 25, for the latest documents, newest first.
4. Call `search_vouchers` with the id as contact_id and voucher_status open, since an open document may be older than the latest ones.
5. Call `get_deeplink` with target contact for a link to the contact, which costs no API call.

Then report who the contact is, their roles with the customer and vendor numbers, and the address. Then what is open, owed to the company and owed by it, as a sum of `openAmount` per currency, with the overdue documents by number and due date. Leave out quotations, order confirmations and delivery notes there, which owe nothing. Then the latest documents as a table with type, number, date, status and total. End with the link.

Ids come from a search result, never from memory. Amounts are exactly what Lexware reports, each with its currency, never rounded and never converted, and a sum is formed per currency. A list answers in pages: read the `page` block and ask for the next page only while `last` is false. Every call spends from one budget of two requests per second. This is a reading task: change nothing in the books, even where a fix looks obvious, and name every gap in the data rather than filling it with a guess. Give no tax advice.
